transcription.tex: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are three events with $P(A)=0.55$, $P(B)=0.35$ and $P(C)=0.4$. $P(A\cap C)=0.2$. Given that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive and $B$ and $C$ are independent,\par a draw a Venn diagram to illustrate the probabilities. (4 marks)\par (b) Find:\par i $P(A'\cap B')$ (1 mark)\par ii $P(A\cup(B\cap C'))$ (1 mark)\par iii $P((A\cap C)'\cup B')$ (1 mark)
(a) \(P(A\cap B)=0\) and \(P(B\cap C)=0.35(0.4)=0.14\). The regions only in \(A,B,C\) are respectively \(0.35,0.21,0.06\). The outside region has probability \(1-0.96=0.04\).
(b)(iii) The complement of \(A\cap C\) omits only that intersection, which lies in \(B^{\prime}\). The required probability is 1.

Given that $A$ and $B$ are independent, $B$ and $C$ are independent, and $A\cap B'\cap C=\varnothing$,\par a draw a Venn diagram to illustrate the probabilities.\par (b) Find:\par i $P(A'\cap(B'\cup C))$     ii $P((A\cup B)\cap C)$\par (c) State, with reasons, whether events $A'$ and $C$ independent.

(a) \(P(A\cap B)=0.25(0.4)=0.1\) and \(P(B\cap C)=0.4(0.45)=0.18\). Subtract the triple intersection: the pair-only regions are \(0,0,0.08\). The single-only regions are \(0.15,0.22,0.27\) and the outside region is \(0.18\).

transcription.tex: Members of a school book club read either murder mysteries ($M$), ghost stories ($G$) or epic fiction ($E$). $P(M)=0.5$, $P(G)=0.4$ and $P(E)=0.6$. Given that no one reads both ghost stories and epic fiction and that $P(M\cap G)=0.3$,\par a draw a Venn diagram to illustrate these probabilities. (4 marks)\par (b) Find:\par i $P(M\cup G)$     ii $P((M\cap G)\cup(M\cap E))$ (2 marks)\par (c) Are the events $G'$ and $M$ independent? You must justify your answer. (2 marks)
(a) \(P(G\cap E)=0\). The \(G\)-only region is \(0.4-0.3=0.1\). Every member outside \(G\) reads \(E\); \(P(M\cap E)=0.5-0.3=0.2\), leaving \(0.4\) in \(E\) only.

transcription.tex: (a) Of 29 students, 23 watch at least one programme and 9 watch \(C\). Hence \(P(C\mid A\cup B\cup C)=\frac{9/29}{23/29}=\frac9{23}\approx0.391\).
(b) Exactly two programmes: \(2+0+1=3\) students. The conditional probability is \(\frac3{23}\approx0.130\).
(c) \(P(B)=\frac{10}{29}\) and \(P(B\mid C)=\frac{1/29}{9/29}=\frac19\). These differ, so \(B,C\) are dependent.

Three events, $A$, $B$ and $C$ are such that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive and $B$ and $C$ are independent. $P(A)=0.2$, $P(B)=0.6$ and $P(C)=0.5$. Given that $P(A'\cap B'\cap C')=0.1$,\par a draw a Venn diagram to show the probabilities for events $A$, $B$ and $C$. (4 marks)\par (b) Find:\par i $P(A\mid C)$ (1 mark)\par ii $P(B\mid C')$ (1 mark)\par iii $P(C\mid(A\cup B))$ (1 mark)

(a) \(P(B\cap C)=0.6(0.5)=0.3\). Only \(B\) has probability \(0.3\). Hence \(P(A\cup C)=1-0.3-0.1=0.6\), giving \(P(A\cap C)=0.2+0.5-0.6=0.1\). The \(A\)-only and \(C\)-only regions each have probability 0.1.

transcription.tex: A doctor completes a medical study of 100 people, 5 of whom are known to have an illness and 95 of whom are known not to. A diagnostic test is applied. All 5 of the people with the illness test positive, and 10 people without the illness also test positive. Given that event $A$ = person has the disease and event $B$ = person tests positive, a draw a Venn diagram to represent this situation. (3 marks)\par (b) Calculate $P(A\mid B)$. (2 marks)\par (c) With reference to your answer to part b, comment on the usefulness of the diagnostic test. (2 marks)
(a) All 5 people with the illness lie in the intersection. Ten more people test positive, and \(100-5-10=85\) are in neither event.
(c) The test found everyone with the illness, but only one third of positive results were true positives in this study.

parts.text: If I were to identify two tips that will possible help you the most in probability questions:
write out the law for conditional probability.
Example: “Given Bob walks to school, find the probability that he’s not late…”
write out the laws for independence.
(Even before you’ve finished reading the question!)

If you’re stuck on a question where you have to find a probability given others, it’s probably because you’ve failed to take into account that two events are independent or mutually exclusive, or you need to use the conditional probability or additional law.

transcription.tex: A box contains 7 sweet and 3 sour jelly beans. Two are selected and eaten. Emilia wants the probability both are sweet given that at least one is sweet.\par She calculates \(P(\text{both sweet})=(7/10)^2=49/100\) and \(P(\text{at least one sweet})=1-(3/10)^2=91/100\). Her answer is \(49/91\).\par Identify her mistake and find the correct probability. (4)

The first bean is eaten, so only 9 remain. If it was sweet, the probability of a second sweet is \(6/9\).\par \(P(\text{both sweet})=\frac7{10}\frac69=\frac7{15}\).\par \(P(\text{at least one sweet})=1-\frac3{10}\frac29=\frac{14}{15}\).\par The required probability is \((7/15)/(14/15)=1/2\).
